Q: Having One Init Function for Structs of Different Data Types A:

Your post contains only one question, so let’s address that first:

But, how am I able to initialise the struct's members if the function has no idea about its members?

First, there is some ambiguity here. Your post talks about malloc and also shows your function init_array_t, so it is not completely clear what you mean by “the function.” I will consider both, in turn.

malloc has no idea about how the contents of the memory will be used; it has no type information at all. It also does not initialize the memory.1

Your routine, init_array_t does have an idea about how the memory will be used because you pass it a parameter, type, that tells it. Your code has a switch for that, so it is unclear why you would ask; the function is clearly set up to do different things for different types.

Let’s also consider something else you mentioned but did not ask as a question:

… more importantly malloc has no way of knowing the required size to allocate memory for the struct.

You tell malloc the size. When you call it, you pass it an argument that says how many bytes to allocate. Your function, init_array_t, would know this because it is passed the type in type. For the case CHAR, it could call malloc using malloc(sizeof (struct string_t)). For another case, it might use malloc(sizeof (struct int8_array_t)).

Footnote

1 To be more specific, it is not specified in the C standard that malloc initializes the memory. It may initialize the memory. What you will find most commonly is that, when malloc gets new memory from the operating system, the operating system has initialized the memory to all zero bits. Then, if that memory is freed in the program and later returned by another malloc, it will contain remnants from whatever data the program used it for and/or data that the memory management routines put into it to help them keep track of freed blocks of memory. In other words, at the time of allocation, malloc will most often not change what is in the memory, whether it is zeros from the operating system, data from the program itself, or data from the memory management routines. Other common behavior you might see is that, when you use a debugging library or turn on debugging features, malloc might fill the memory with some characteristic pattern to aid in detection of otherwise uninitialized memory.
